Patient_Profile:
1. A woman in her 60s with a history of hyperlipidemia, hypothyroidism, and chronic migraines presented with 9 months of progressively worsening left-sided ptosis, which was more notable at night and with fatigue.
2. She denied experiencing pain, diplopia, muscle weakness, dysarthria, dysphagia, difficulty breathing, or other neurologic deficits.
3. On examination, corrected visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally, with normal color vision, visual fields, intraocular pressure, extraocular movements, alignment, and pupils.
4. External examination was notable for left upper eyelid ptosis (Figure 1), with a margin-to-reflex distance 1 of 3.5 mm on the right and 0.5 mm on the left, intact levator function, and no fatiguability on sustained upgaze.
5. There was no evidence of eyelid edema, erythema, or tenderness to palpation.
6. There were no palpable adnexal masses or orbital rim deformities, but there was mild fullness in the left superior sulcus and mildly increased left-sided resistance to retropulsion.
7. However, Hertel exophthalmometry did not reveal any relative proptosis.
8. No lacrimal gland abnormalities or conjunctival masses were seen with upper eyelid eversion.
9. There was no palpable preauricular or cervical lymphadenopathy.
10. Slitlamp and fundus examination findings were normal.
11. Serological testing results for antiacetylcholine receptor antibody were negative.

2. Following neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, low anterior resection, and 6 cycles of adjuvant FOLFOX therapy (fluorouracil, leucovorin, and oxaliplatin), he had developed a lung metastasis (KRAS wild type) 1 year later.
3. He subsequently developed multiple lung metastases treated with palliative local interventions (lobectomy, radiofrequency ablation) and 4 lines of chemotherapy.
4. Owing to symptomatic lung disease, he was enrolled in a clinical trial (NCT03502733) following informed consent and achieved a confirmed partial response.
5. After 9 months, contrast computed tomography restaging scans noted a new, 1-cm posterior subglottic lesion of unclear origin (Figure, A).
6. He had no shortness of breath or noisy breathing, dysphagia, voice change, or hemoptysis.
7. A partial response was maintained without evidence of progression of lung disease.A, An axial computed tomographic image reveals a new posterior subglottic lesion (pink arrowhead) of unclear etiology.
8. B, In the operating room, the larynx was exposed with a Lindholm laryngoscope, and a Hopkins rod-lens endoscope was used to photograph the lesion under apneic conditions.
9. C, Photomicrograph (original magnification ×20) of a section of the mass stained for CDX2 via standard immunohistochemical techniques.Otolaryngology was consulted to assess the lesion.
10. The differential diagnosis based on imaging included a mass vs inspissated mucus.
11. Examination using distal-chip flexible laryngoscopy revealed a 1-cm, broad-based, exophytic mass along the posterior wall of the subglottis with prominent vasculature.
12. No other anatomic abnormalities in the upper aerodigestive tract or cervical lymphadenopathy were noted.
13. The decision was made to proceed to the operating room for definitive endoscopic biopsy under general anesthesia (Figure, B).
14. Examination revealed a subglottic mass that did not extend inferiorly beyond the caudal aspect of the cricoid cartilage.
15. The mass was debulked and sent to pathology for analysis, including hematoxylin-eosin and immunohistochemical staining (Figure, C).

1. A man in his early 30s presented with 4 days of acute, monocular, painless vision loss.  
2. His visual acuity was 20/200 OD and 20/20 OS.

8. He had fevers and mild upper respiratory tract symptoms 2 weeks before his presentation, closely followed by a rash on his hands and thighs.  
9. A young family member had similar symptoms.Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) revealed a fovea-involving neurosensory retinal detachment, outer photoreceptor thickening, and an intact external limiting membrane overlying a zone of mildly thickened, irregular RPE.  
10. The submacular choroid was relatively thick bilaterally on enhanced depth imaging OCT (Figure 1B).  
11. Combined fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography demonstrated mottled early hyperfluorescence with late staining and minimal pooling.  
12. There was no leakage from the retinal vessels or optic discs bilaterally, and uninvolved areas of RPE and choroidal vasculature were unremarkable.  
13. A test for rapid plasma reagin was negative.Observe; follow up in 4 to 6 weeks with SD-OCTTreat with intravitreal antivascular endothelial growth factor injection

Patient_Profile:
1. A 50-year-old man was referred for ophthalmoplegia that developed immediately after an 8.5-hour robotic cystectomy for small cell cancer of the bladder.  
2. After recovering from anesthesia in the postanesthesia care unit, he experienced headache, facial numbness, inability to open both his eyes, and inability to move both eyes in any direction.  
3. He had a known enhancing central skull base lesion in sella turcica with compression of the optic chiasm and mild mass effect on the pons that was felt to be a pituitary macroadenoma (Figure).  
4. His baseline examination before the cystectomy showed visual acuity of 20/20 OU with intact extraocular movements and unremarkable confrontational fields, although a mild bitemporal hemianopia was seen on automated visual fields.  
5. T1-weighted coronal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with contrast shows a 4.9 × 4.6 × 5.2-cm sellar/parasellar lobulated mass with homogenous enhancement before symptom onset (A), which became 5.3 × 5.1 × 5.3 cm and had loss of enhancement after symptom onset (B).  
6. The mass caused superior displacement of the optic chiasm and had extension into the cavernous sinus bilaterally.  
7. The mass also extended posteriorly and deformed the anterior aspect of the pons (not shown).  
8. After symptom onset, the mass was hyperintense on T2-weighted images (not shown).  
9. During the bedside examination in the postanesthesia care unit, he was noted to have complete bilateral ptosis.  
10. His visual acuity was 20/20 OU with full visual fields on confrontational visual field testing.  
11. He had decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in the V1/V2 distribution of the trigeminal nerve bilaterally.  
12. The right and left pupils were 5 mm and 6 mm in size, respectively, in both light and dark.  
13. There was no pupillary response to light or accommodation.  
14. No exophthalmos was noted.  
15. Intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes.  
16. The patient was unable to move either eye in any direction on extraocular motility testing.  
17. Vestibulo-ocular reflex did not overcome the ophthalmoplegia.  
18. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was obtained 12 hours after symptom onset redemonstrating the large sellar mass, which no longer had central enhancement (Figure).

10. Biopsy of the mandible showed the same type of tissue as seen in the right femur and tibia.

1. An Asian woman in her 50s with diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presented with ptosis and intermittent esotropia of the right eye.  
2. Fourteen years earlier, the patient underwent a pituitary adenoma resection and external beam radiation.  
3. Immediately after the resection, she developed slight ptosis and an adduction deficit of the right eye, presumed to be secondary to partial oculomotor nerve III (CNIII) damage.  
4. Four years earlier, she developed intermittent esotropia of the right eye, presumed secondary to cranial nerve VI palsy.  
5. At the present clinic visit, the patient reported the persistence of intermittent diplopia, which had remained unchanged for years, and denied other ocular or systemic complaints.  
6. Visual acuity measured 20/20 OU.  
7. We noted 3 mm of relative right upper eyelid ptosis and anisocoria (3 mm OD and 4.5 mm OS in ambient lighting).  
8. Pupils were round and reactive with no afferent pupillary defect.  
9. The degree of anisocoria was the same in ambient and dim lighting.  
10. Extraocular movements were initially intact; however, a few minutes later, the patient developed an intermittent esotropia of the right eye, with episodes of sustained adduction lasting up to 30 seconds followed by normalization of ductions and alignment (Video; Figure, A).  
11. These episodes occurred more commonly following voluntary adduction.  
12. On infraduction, the right upper eyelid simultaneously retracted, exposing 3 mm of superior sclera (Figure, B).  
13. On adduction, the right pupil constricted slightly.  
14. The remainder of the examination was within normal limits.  
15. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) from 1 year prior showed a small amount of residual tumor within the right cavernous sinus, stable over years (Figure, C).

Patient_Profile:
1. A 55-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with several weeks of malaise and a 6.8-kg weight loss associated with poor appetite.
2. He reported no fevers, night sweats, abdominal pain, emesis, and diarrhea.
3. Physical examination revealed a thin habitus; no palmar erythema, spider angiomas, or gynecomastia were observed.
4. Laboratory tests showed normal complete blood cell count and chemistry panel findings.
5. Hepatic panel showed an elevated alkaline phosphatase level (209 U/L; upper limit of normal [ULN], 150 U/L [3.49 μkat/L; ULN, 2.5 μkat/L]), normal total bilirubin level (0.4 mg/dL [6.84 μmol/L]), elevated alanine aminotransferase level (41 U/L; ULN, 35 U/L [0.68 μkat/L; ULN, 0.58 μkat/L]), and normal aspartate aminotransferase level (27 U/L [0.45 μkat/L]).
6. A single-phase computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen revealed multiple hypoattenuating masses with rim enhancement throughout the liver, intussusception of the small bowel, and normal liver contour with no signs of portal hypertension (Figure 1, left). α-Fetoprotein (AFP) level was elevated (1252 ng/mL; ULN, 9 ng/mL); levels of carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (<2 U/mL) and carcinoembryonic antigen (2.8 ng/mL) were normal.
7. A triple-phase CT scan was obtained to further evaluate the small bowel, which revealed no small bowel abnormalities but instead demonstrated a 3.3 × 2.8-cm heterogeneously enhancing pancreatic tail mass not seen on the previous single-phase CT (Figure 1, right).
8. Left, Axial view from single-phase computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen revealing bilobar liver masses.
9. Right, Coronal view from venous phase of triple-phase CT scan revealing a pancreatic tail mass (arrowhead) in addition to the bilobar liver masses.

6. The patient lived with her family, including her son who recently had a cough.  
7. She was born in the Philippines and immigrated to the United States 3 decades prior.  
8. She denied recent travel.  
9. On examination, her temperature was 38.3° C, pulse of 115 beats/min, blood pressure of 110/50 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 24 breaths/min, and an oxygen saturation of 90% on room air.

11. Her laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 4.2 × 106/mL (normal range, 3.4-10 × 106/mL), hemoglobin of 10.3 g/dL (normal range, 12-15.5 g/dL [to convert g/dL to g/L, multiply by 10]), platelets of 45 × 106/mL (normal range, 140-450 × 106/mL), and creatinine of 1.2 mg/dL (normal range, 0.5-1.0 mg/dL [to convert mg/dL to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4]).  
12. A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral opacities without pleural effusion or pneumothorax.  
13. Initial empirical treatment included vancomycin, cefepime, azithromycin, and oseltamivir.  
14. On hospital day 2, she was intubated for hypoxemic respiratory failure.  
15. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest was performed (Figure, A) and compared with a study 2 weeks prior when she was asymptomatic (Figure, B).  
16. A, Computed tomographic (CT) chest image obtained on admission demonstrates diffuse bilateral ground glass opacities with interlobular septal thickening.  
17. B, Computed tomographic chest image from 2 weeks prior demonstrates nearly normal lungs.

1. A 31-year-old gravida 1, para 1 woman with a history of Wolff-Parkinson-White disease and recently diagnosed stage II Hodgkin lymphoma presented with a pruritic rash.
2. She was diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma at 35 weeks’ gestation, and 1 week later she underwent cesarean delivery.
3. At 3 weeks’ postpartum, she began chemotherapy (cycle 1, day 1) with adriamycin, bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine (ABVD).
4. On day 15 of cycle 1, she presented with linear, hyperpigmented streaks and welts on her arms, back, and legs.
5. Intense, diffuse pruritus had developed within 24 hours of the patient’s first day of treatment, and her symptoms were poorly responsive to antihistamines and topical steroids.
6. Pruritus was followed by the appearance of dark scratch marks as demonstrated in the Figure.
7. Laboratory test results revealed a white blood cell count of 1.6 ×103 cells/mm3, with an absolute neutrophil count of 500 cells/mm3 and a total bilirubin of 0.3 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 17.104), which was unchanged from the baseline total bilirubin.
8. Clinical photograph of the patient’s back shows scratch marks that appeared after diffuse pruritus.

12. Staging imaging revealed bilateral supraclavicular jugular chain, paratracheal and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 67 mm/h.
13. She was diagnosed with stage II, unfavorable-risk Hodgkin lymphoma.

9. There was an associated thick fibrotic epiretinal membrane extending from the macula to the superior peripheral retina.

12. Fluorescein angiography of her right eye showed early hyperfluorescence of the lesions with late leakage (Figure 1B).

14. Associated engorged and tortuous vessels emanate from the optic disc.

5. Her last colonoscopy was 3 years ago, and UC without evidence of dysplasia was confirmed.
6. Otherwise, her medical history was unremarkable.
7. Family history was negative for inflammatory bowel diseases and gastrointestinal malignancies.

9. Her abdomen was tender to palpation in the left lower quadrant, which was soft and nondistended.
10. The patient’s complete blood cell count and comprehensive metabolic panel results were unremarkable.

12. There was also a 2.7-cm intramural abscess in the descending colon.

15. She underwent a colonoscopy, which demonstrated multiple areas of inflammation in the rectum through the descending colon (Figure 1).

Patient_Profile:
1. A 72-year-old man presented with mild proximal weakness developing into progressive camptocormia, head drop, and prominent dysphagia over a 2-year period.
2. He reported a 20-kg weight loss and numbness to the ankles.
3. His medical history was significant for thyroid cancer treated with total thyroidectomy resulting in a chronic left accessory nerve injury, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and gout.
4. His medications were metformin, allopurinol, perindopril, thyroxine, and rabeprazole.
5. He had no history of smoking and drank 3 glasses of wine per week.
6. His family history was unremarkable.
7. Examination revealed significant wasting of proximal and paraspinal muscles with a flexed spine posture in the upright position (Figure 1A).
8. He had symmetric Medical Research Council grade 4/5 weakness of neck flexion, shoulder abduction, elbow flexion and extension, and hip flexion and extension bilaterally.
9. He had weakness of left shoulder elevation and winging of the left scapula secondary to the accessory nerve injury.
10. His deep tendon reflexes were normal and symmetric.
11. Pinprick sensation was reduced in both feet.
12. Lateral profile of the patient (A) revealing a flexed spine posture (camptocormia) with marked generalized muscle atrophy.
13. B, A Gömöri trichrome stain of frozen left vastus muscle (original magnification ×400) reveals 3 atrophic muscle fibers with a patchy granular appearance (red arrowheads).
14. Metabolic, endocrine, autoimmune, and infectious screens had unremarkable findings.
15. Creatine kinase levels were normal.
16. A myositis panel demonstrated low-positive Mi2 antibodies.
17. Serum electrophoresis and immunofixation identified a small immunoglobulin G (IgG) κ paraprotein with normal findings on bone marrow biopsy.
18. A whole-body positron emission tomography scan was normal.
19. Nerve conduction studies revealed a mild axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy.
20. Concentric needle electromyography showed no spontaneous activity with widespread small, brief, polyphasic units, particularly in proximal and axial muscles, consistent with a myopathic process.
21. An initial deltoid muscle biopsy did not show evidence of myopathy.
22. Because the patient’s symptoms were worsening, a second muscle biopsy of vastus lateralis was performed.

9. No lymphadenopathy of the inguinal region was noted.

Patient_Profile:
1. A 46-year-old healthy Hispanic woman presented with 2 days of photophobia in her right eye.
2. Her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/30 + 2 OD and 20/20 OS.
3. Her intraocular pressure, extraocular motility, and pupillary light reactions were normal.
4. An examination demonstrated trace anterior cells in the right eye; otherwise, the examination had normal results.
5. No vitreous cells were present.
6. Topical prednisolone was started for presumed acute anterior uveitis.
7. One week later, the photophobia had improved.
8. However, unnoticed by the patient, her BCVA had worsened to 20/200 OD and 20/40 OS.
9. An examination demonstrated new subretinal fluid in the macula in the right eye (Figure 1A).
10. Fluorescein angiography showed peripapillary speckled pinpoint areas of hyperfluorescence in the right eye.
11. Indocyanine green showed early choroidal vessel hyperfluorescence and several posterior focal hypofluorescent spots in the midphase in both eyes.
12. Autofluorescence showed patchy hyperautofluorescence in both eyes.
13. Tuberculosis and syphilis testing had negative results.
14. A complete blood cell count was unremarkable.
15. A diagnosis of central serous retinopathy (CSR) was made.
16. The topical prednisolone was stopped.
17. Findings on presentation and follow-up.
18. A, Optical coherence tomography of the right eye demonstrates posterior vitreous cells (white arrowheads), subretinal fluid, and choroidal corrugation (yellow arrowheads).
19. B, Fundus photograph of the right eye demonstrates multifocal, demarcated exudative retinal detachments, including in the macula.
20. Similar findings were present in the left eye.
21. One week later, the BCVA worsened to E at 3 feet OD and 20/200 OS.
22. An examination now revealed 2+ vitreous cells and extensive exudative retinal detachments in both eyes (Figure 1B).
23. No retinal tears were seen on a depressed examination.
24. Retinal detachment repair with vitrectomy and/or scleral buckle

Patient_Profile:
1. A man in his early 70s with 2 months of progressive dimming of his vision was referred for evaluation.
2. He initially presented to his primary care physician reporting unintentional weight loss, fevers, and subacute visual decline.
3. Subsequent ophthalmic examination revealed mild anterior and posterior inflammation, raising suspicion for panuveitis.
4. Results of laboratory tests for sarcoidosis, Lyme disease, and syphilis were negative.
5. However, a right upper lobe lung mass noted on the chest radiograph proved to be T2N2M0 stage III non–small-cell lung cancer on biopsy.
6. On presentation to us, the patient’s visual acuity was 20/150 OD and 20/200 OS, but improved to 20/70 OU with pinhole.
7. He was pseudophakic with bilateral mild anterior chamber inflammation, moderate vitreous haze, and inferior vitreous condensations.
8. The posterior pole demonstrated bilateral diffuse retinal pigment epithelial alterations with a prominent leopard spot pattern and focal choroidal pigmented lesions.
9. Macular subretinal fluid tracked to the inferior periphery in both eyes (Figure 1A).
10. Optical coherence tomography confirmed bilateral subretinal fluid and retinal pigment epithelial irregularity (Figure 1B); nummular hypoautofluorescent lesions were interspersed within areas of hyperautofluorescence on autofluorescence imaging.
11. The optic disc and peripheral vasculature leaked on fluorescein angiography.
12. B-scan ultrasonography also showed diffuse choroidal thickening with focal choroidal thickening consistent with the pigmented choroidal lesions.
13. Ultrasonographic biomicroscopy revealed ciliary cysts associated with anterior thickening of both ciliary bodies.
14. A, Optos photograph of the left eye demonstrating diffuse retinal pigment epithelial alterations in a leopard spot pattern (white arrowhead) and focal choroidal pigmented lesions, as well as subretinal fluid that tracks to the inferior periphery.
15. B, Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula of the left eye demonstrating subretinal fluid (asterisk) with areas of retinal pigment epithelium loss (yellow arrowhead) and irregular thickening (white arrowhead).
16. Pars plana vitrectomy with drainage of subretinal fluid

2. She noted mild associated pruritus but denied burning sensation.
3. The eruptions occurred intermittently, appearing as erythematous papules with prominent pustules, and were exacerbated by sunlight.
4. On average, her lesions would resolve in 3 to 4 days with only mild background erythema by 5 to 7 days.
5. Even mild sun exposure would induce the eruption, leading to frequent recurrences in summer months but long periods of remission in the fall through spring.
6. Trials with various broad-spectrum sunscreens in combination with topical and oral antibiotics and topical ivermectin did not prevent flares or mitigate severity of eruptions when they occurred.
7. She denied joint pain, fever, fatigue, changes in urine color, use of other topical or systemic medications, or presence of rashes elsewhere.
8. She was otherwise healthy without other medical history.
9. On physical examination, she was well appearing with numerous 1- to 2-mm monomorphous pustules over background erythema on the medial cheeks, chin, and nose (Figure, A).
10. No nail fold capillary changes or mucosal lesions were observed.
11. Serum analysis results for antinuclear, anti-SSA/Ro, and anti-SSB/La antibodies were negative.
12. A 4-mm punch biopsy was taken from a representative lesion along the right jawline (Figure, B-D).
13. A, Pustular eruption of the face characterized by monomorphous 1- to 2-mm pustules over background erythema on the cheeks, chin, and nose appearing less than 24 hours after sun exposure.
14. Punch biopsy of skin demonstrated intrafollicular (B and C) and subcorneal (B and D) pustule formation (hematoxylin-eosin).

1. A woman in her 60s presented 1 week after undergoing cataract surgery in the right eye complaining of persistent blurry vision.
2. Her ocular history was notable for a previous uncomplicated cataract surgery in the left eye that had a good visual outcome.
3. On postoperative day 1, her visual acuity was 20/60 OD, attributed to mild corneal edema, with an intraocular pressure of 18 mm Hg.
4. A dilated fundus examination was not performed.
5. At postoperative week 1, the best-corrected visual acuity was 20/50 OD, her intraocular pressure was 17 mm Hg, and there was no afferent pupillary defect.
6. The cornea was clear and there were trace anterior chamber cells.
7. A dilated examination revealed multiple spots of retinal whitening with tiny intraretinal hemorrhages concentrated in the posterior pole (Figure, A).
8. The patient was referred urgently for consultation by a retina specialist.
9. Optical coherence tomography revealed intraretinal cystoid abnormalities in the macula and hyperreflective patches in the nerve fiber layer and inner nuclear layer (Figure, B).
10. A, Fundus photograph of the right eye demonstrating multifocal patches of inner retinal whitening in the posterior pole.
11. B, Optical coherence tomography through the macula demonstrating mild intraretinal cystoid abnormalities and hyperreflective thickened areas in the nerve fiber and inner nuclear layer, corresponding to the white retinal patches.

1. A previously healthy 12-year-old boy presented to an outside hospital for fever, headache, and unilateral red eye with periorbital edema.  
2. He received oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and 2 days of intravenous clindamycin phosphate and ceftriaxone sodium.

9. The pediatrics service planned to restart antibiotic therapy.  
10. External photograph of the left eye demonstrating periorbital edema, lash crusting, and follicular conjunctivitis with a granuloma in the inferolateral fornix.  
11. Perform conjunctival cultures on blood, chocolate, Löwenstein-Jensen, Sabouraud, and thioglycolate media before restarting antibiotic therapy.  
12. Provide reassurance that the diagnosis is typically self-limited.  
13. Perform serologic testing for Bartonella henselae and Francisella tularensis

4. Ophthalmoscopy revealed bilateral swollen, hyperemic optic discs with multifocal yellowish choroidal lesions located at the midperiphery and posterior pole of the retina.
5. The lesions varied in size, ranging from one-fourth to twice the diameter of the optic disc.

7. Results of fundus fluorescein angiography showed bilateral early hypofluorescence, with late staining and leakage from the optic discs.

9. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated, at 80 mm/h, as was the C-reactive protein level, at 20.2 mg/L (to convert to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 9.524).
10. Chest radiograph showed consolidation in the right lower zone (Figure 1B).
11. However, results of tuberculin skin test, sputum for acid-fast bacilli, and sputum culture were negative.
12. Three days after initial presentation, the patient developed acute binocular horizontal diplopia and disorientation.
13. A, Color fundus photograph revealed bilateral swollen, hyperemic optic discs with multifocal choroidal lesions.
14. B, Chest radiograph showed consolidation in the right lower zone.

11. No contractures or webbing of fingers was noted.  
12. There was no organomegaly.

11. On the left medial thigh, there was a large indurated, tender red-brown plaque.
12. Wound cultures and polymerase chain reaction studies from the right forearm were negative for herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus infections.
13. Punch biopsy specimens from lesions on the scalp, right forearm, and left thigh were sent for histopathological and immunohistochemical assessment and tissue culture (Figure, B-D).

1. A 5-year-old girl was referred to a pediatric gastroenterology clinic for chronic constipation and poor weight gain.  
2. During her first week of life, she developed diarrhea and vomiting.  
3. With initiation of solid food, she developed laxative-dependent constipation.  
4. She underwent newborn genetic screening before routine cystic fibrosis (CF) screening.  
5. Results were normal.  
6. At the time of presentation to the gastroenterology clinic, she had no respiratory symptoms.  
7. Results of anorectal manometry, spinal magnetic resonance imaging, and thyroid studies were normal.  
8. Family history included constipation in a sister and a great aunt with CF.  
9. Her body mass index (BMI) was below the third percentile (eFigureA in the Supplement).  
10. Physical examination findings were unremarkable, including normal respiratory examination.  
11. Fecal elastase level was within reference range (>500 μg/g); abdominal computed tomographic image revealed a dilated, tortuous sigmoid colon; and full-thickness rectal biopsy was negative for Hirschsprung disease.  
12. She was referred for sweat chloride testing to assess for CF.  
13. Results of 3 separate sweat chloride tests were indeterminate (Table), prompting pulmonology referral.  
14. A 97-mutation CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) analysis panel was negative.  
15. Whole-genome sequence analysis revealed 1 CF-causing mutation (c.2249C>T) and 2 likely benign variants (c.1408A>G and c.2562T>G).  
16. No further testing; the patient does not have CF

4. The nodule first appeared 1 year prior.

9. The nodule was rock-hard, with a friable yellow-red plaque between the nodule and ostomy site.
10. The stoma was red, moist, and well-perfused.

Patient_Profile:
1. A 75-year-old woman presenting with decreased visual acuity and metamorphopsia in the right eye was referred for further evaluation of a pigmented epiretinal membrane.
2. She had a history of cutaneous nodular melanoma in the right arm.
3. Tumor staging was classified as T3N0M0 in August 2017, at the time of diagnosis and excision.
4. In April 2018, axillary lymphadenectomy was performed for local recurrence and the patient started treatment with an immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) pembrolizumab, without further local or metastatic evidence of the tumor.
5. Ocular history was positive for cataract surgery bilaterally.
6. After cataract surgery in the right eye, an asymptomatic vision loss was noted and the cause was attributed to the presence of choroidal neovascularization (CNV), for which the patient underwent intravitreal anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injections.
7. Examination showed a best-corrected visual acuity of 20/60 OD and 20/20 OS, unremarkable anterior segment findings, and intraocular pressures of 12 mm Hg OU.
8. A fundus examination in the right eye revealed scarce pigmented cells in the anterior vitreous, a dark-pigmented epiretinal membrane, and an area of retinal hyperpigmentation in the inferior temporal arcade corresponding to the CNV.
9. Optical coherence tomography imaging revealed a hyperreflective structure on the surface of the inner retina with increased macular thickness, compatible with the described epiretinal membrane.
10. Fundus examination in the right eye revealed scarce pigmented cells in the anterior vitreous, a dark-pigmented epiretinal membrane, and an area of retinal hyperpigmentation in the inferior temporal arcade corresponding to the choroidal neovascularization.

Patient_Profile:
1. A man in his 50s with a history of hypertension and sleep apnea presented with a 6-week history of progressive, bilateral vision loss while receiving treatment with oral steroids and amoxicillin-clavulanate from his primary care physician.  
2. He also had associated ear pain, hearing loss, and severe headaches.  
3. On presentation, his visual acuity was light perception OD and 20/600 at 1 m OS.  
4. The right eye had a 1+ afferent pupillary defect.  
5. He also had ear drainage with inflamed tympanic membranes and ear tubes in place bilaterally.  
6. A dilated fundus examination revealed grade 2 optic disc edema with an inferior disc hemorrhage in the right eye and grade 1 edema in the left eye.  
7. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.  
8. Laboratory results revealed elevated C-reactive protein levels and erythrocyte sedimentation rates at 78 mg/L and 77 mm/h, respectively, with negative antinuclear antibody test results (to convert C-reactive protein to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 9.524).  
9. His white blood cell count was elevated at 14 910/μL without eosinophilia (to convert to × 109/L, multiply by 0.001).  
10. Cerebrospinal fluid studies were remarkable only for an elevated white blood cell count of 72/μL (79% lymphocytes) and elevated protein level at 97 mg/L, while Gram stain and culture were negative.  
11. Opening pressure was 17 cm H2O.  
12. A magnetic resonance venogram with and without contrast ruled out venous occlusions.  
13. Finally, magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated diffuse pachymeningeal (dural-arachnoid) enhancement (Figure) without leptomeningeal (pial) enhancement, left-sided mastoiditis, and subtle optic nerve enhancement.  
14. Coronal T1 with gadolinium showing dural enhancement (blue arrowhead) and optic nerve enhancement (white arrowheads).

1. A healthy man in his 60s presented with a 4-month history of blurred vision in his left eye.  
2. On examination, his visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/40 OS.  
3. Intraocular pressures were normal in each eye.  
4. Anterior segment and fundus examination results were normal in the right eye.  
5. In the left eye, the media were clear, and there were multiple patchy, yellow choroidal lesions with obliteration of the normal choroidal vasculature throughout the entire fundus (Figure 1A).  
6. There was no sign of vitritis or retinitis and no history of previous trauma, uveitis, sarcoidosis, or cancer.  
7. Ocular ultrasonography revealed diffuse ciliochoroidal thickening measuring 2.9 mm in elevation.  
8. Optical coherence tomography disclosed generalized, undulating choroidal infiltration in a seasick pattern, so to speak, given its resemblance to a stormy ocean surface, with overlying draping of the retina in the foveal region (Figure 1B).  
9. A relook at the anterior segment in the left eye revealed a faint conjunctival thickening at the limbus suggestive of lymphoid tumor.  
10. Incisional biopsy of the epibulbar lesion revealed sheetlike infiltration of small monomorphic lymphocytes with irregular nuclear contours and Dutcher bodies.  
11. Initiate an oral corticosteroid plus intravitreal anti–vascular endothelial growth factor therapy Administer topical interferon 4 times a day for 3 months Complete serum immunoglobulin level tests, DNA molecular analysis, and bone marrow biopsy

Patient_Profile:
1. A 13-year-old boy with a longstanding history of gait imbalance presented with 2 episodes of acute-onset left hemibody weakness and dysarthria without changes in sensorium in a 24-hour period.  
2. Symptoms lasted approximately 60 minutes each before completely resolving; prior to the day of the events, he had never experienced similar phenomena.  
3. Initial examination following the second event revealed mild-to-moderate dysarthria, pes planovalgus and tight achilles tendons bilaterally, and decreased vibratory and fine touch sensation from the great toe up to the mid shin bilaterally.  
4. Reflexes were absent at the patella and achilles bilaterally.  
5. Bilateral dorsiflexion weakness was present (4 of 5).  
6. There were otherwise no motor deficits, muscle atrophy, or lateralizing neurologic abnormalities.  
7. On arrival, the patient underwent a stroke/transient ischemic attack workup.  
8. Results of a comprehensive metabolic panel, complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and a coagulation panel were within normal limits.  
9. Computed tomography angiogram demonstrated no evidence of extra or intracranial dissection.  
10. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with and without contrast (Figure) demonstrated symmetric, bilateral, restricted diffusion, with T2 hyperintensities in the supratentorial white matter and corpus callosum.  
11. Lumbar puncture was obtained and revealed normal cell counts and no oligoclonal bands or evidence of infection.  
12. A, Diffusion-weighted imaging sequence demonstrating bilateral, symmetric, restricted diffusion of the supratentorial white matter (corresponding hypointensity noted on apparent diffusion coefficient sequences).  
13. B, T2 sequence demonstrating bilateral and symmetric increased signal in the supratenorial white matter–sparing U-fibers.  
14. The patient had reportedly always walked on the outside of his feet and had been considered clumsy when compared with other children but had no history of motor delays.  
15. Family history revealed a mother with diminished reflexes, hand tremor, and balance issues with a prior inconclusive electromyogram and nerve conduction study.  
16. A younger brother with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder also had similar gait abnormalities.

1. A woman in her 20s presented with sudden-onset visual loss of the right eye for 1 day.

6. She had no other abnormal neurologic signs or symptoms.  
7. Results of slitlamp examination were normal.  
8. A relative afferent pupillary defect 1+ was noted in the right eye.  
9. Dilated fundus examination showed no evidence of vitritis, optic nerve swelling, or retinal pigment epithelial abnormalities.  
10. Automated visual field testing showed a central scotoma in the right eye, and the visual evoked potential showed a delayed P100 response in the right eye.  
11. Results of an initial ophthalmologic workup, including fundus photography and fluorescence angiography, were considered to be unremarkable.  
12. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbit revealed no enhancement of the optic nerves.  
13. At a subsequent visit, 2 small glistening lesions in the retina were identified, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed an attenuated ellipsoid zone at a position nasal to the fovea (Figure 1).  
14. Fundus photography shows 2 small glistening lesions (white arrowheads) (A).  
15. Disrupted ellipsoid zone at the fovea was noted on optical coherence tomography (red arrowheads) (B).  
16. Search for nematodes under a high-magnification fundus contact lens examination

1. A previously healthy man in his 40s presented with 4 days of fever and a rash.
2. He noticed multiple acneiform papules and pustules around the neckline that progressed to involve the face, torso, and limbs.
3. He took no prescribed medications but had taken an ibuprofen pill a week prior for a mild headache; his symptoms started 3 days after that.
4. He had no sick contacts or recent travel and reported no use of alcohol or tobacco.
5. On examination, he was febrile (38.9°C) and tachycardic but normotensive.
6. Clusters of pustules, approximately 1 mm in diameter, were present over an erythematous base overlying the face, neck, chest, back, and arms (Figure).
7. Laboratory analysis revealed values within normal ranges for hemoglobin (13.1 g/dL) and platelet count (186 ×109/L); an elevated white blood cell count (22.3 x109/L; 82% neutrophils, 9% lymphocytes, 5% eosinophils, 4% monocytes); erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 58 mm/h (reference range, 0-20); C-reactive protein level of 232 mg/L (2210 nmol/L) (reference, <5 mg/dL [48 nmol/L]); and normal renal and hepatic function.
8. Gram stain of the pustule fluid revealed no organisms, and cultures of the blood and pustule fluid were without growth.
9. A punch biopsy of the skin lesions showed subcorneal pustules containing neutrophils and eosinophils, with epidermal spongiosis.

6. Dilated fundus examination revealed a small peripheral hypoautofluorescent chorioretinal scar in the right eye.
7. In the left eye, there was trace vitreous haze and 2+ anterior vitreous cell.
8. Multifocal chorioretinal scars extended from the left optic nerve into the macula in each quadrant (Figure 1).
9. These lesions showed variable hypoautofluorescence and hyperautofluorescence.

12. A chest radiograph was normal.Fundus photograph of the left eye demonstrating multifocal outer retinal lesions with variable pigmentation extending from the optic nerve to the equator with sparing of the foveal center.
13. Lesions are surrounded by yellow borders with a patch of prominent choriocapillary atrophy nasal and superior to the nerve.

5. His best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 OD and 20/30 OS.

10. Patient_Profile:
1. A 62-year-old woman with a history of chronic angle-closure glaucoma and bilateral peripheral iridotomies sought a second opinion for worsening visual acuity in the left eye for 2 months.
2. She had been treated for glaucoma for approximately 1 year.
3. Review of systems was negative for previous episodes of eye pain, redness, or emesis.
4. Her medical history included hyperlipidemia, obesity, and prior cataract surgery in both eyes.
5. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/80 OS.
6. The patient’s pupils were equal, round, and reactive to light without a relative afferent pupillary defect.
7. Intraocular pressure was 11 mm Hg bilaterally without medication.
8. Slitlamp findings were notable for patent peripheral iridotomies, open angles on gonioscopy, and an asymmetrically enlarged cup-disc ratio with mild pallor of the left optic nerve.
9. Color vision was decreased in the left eye.
10. Visual field (VF) testing as well as ganglion cell layer (GCL) segmentation by optical coherence tomography (OCT) were obtained for both eyes (Figure 1).
11. Optical coherence tomography ganglion cell layer thickness map shows nasal thinning of the right eye (A) and diffuse thinning of the left eye (B).
12. In the right eye, the relative thinning within the nasal macula compared with the temporal macula suggests injury to the papillomacular bundle.
13. In the left eye, the diffuse thinning suggests diffuse optic nerve injury (Heidelberg Spectralis; Heidelberg).
14. Insets show Humphrey 24-2 perimetry with minimal nonspecific defects in the right eye and a temporal scotoma in the left eye.
15. Refer to a retina specialist owing to retinal thinning Start intraocular pressure–lowering medications owing to GCL loss

Patient_Profile:
1. A 32-year-old Nigerian woman presented with dull pain, pruritus, and discoloration of the dorsal aspect of both feet for 18 months.
2. Her medical history included a red blood cell transfusion as a child and 2 uncomplicated pregnancies.
3. The lesions started as small papules on the dorsal right great toe and left third toe that gradually spread across the dorsum of her feet over the following 12 months.
4. An over-the-counter antifungal ointment was unhelpful.
5. Her primary care physician completed a biopsy, diagnosed verruca plantaris, and prescribed topical salicylic acid twice daily for 4 weeks.
6. The lesions did not improve, and her foot pain worsened.
7. Subsequent treatment with topical liquid nitrogen cryotherapy was ineffective.
8. Three months after cryotherapy, the patient presented to the dermatology clinic regarding the lesions on her feet.
9. The patient stated that the lesions had been stable in size for the previous 6 months, without bleeding, discharge, or change in color.
10. She continued to have 6 of 10, dull, constant pain that was nonradiating, improved when she soaked her feet in water, and worsened with any type of topical pressure or wrapping.
11. Physical examination revealed multiple well-circumscribed, scaly plaques with cobblestone surfaces on the dorsal aspects of the forefoot and midfoot bilaterally.
12. Findings were more severe on the right and left hindfoot (Figure, left panel).
13. On serologic testing, the patient was negative for HIV and positive for hepatitis C virus (HCV).
14. A punch biopsy of the right foot lesion revealed psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia, parakeratosis, eosinophils, papillary dermal inflammation, and intraepidermal necrosis (Figure, right panel).
15. Left, Dorsal aspects of bilateral forefoot and midfoot of a 32-year-old Nigerian woman.
16. Right, Punch biopsy of the patient’s right foot lesion (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×40).

4. Papillae were also noted bilaterally on the superior palpebral conjunctiva.
5. He did not report any redness or discharge but did note mildly increased irritation mainly from soft contact lens wear.
6. He had endorsed proper contact lens care and hygiene.
7. He also noted an upper respiratory tract illness 4 weeks before presentation.
8. Initially, he received a giant papillary conjunctivitis diagnosis because of soft contact lens intolerance and a recommendation to take a contact lens break.
9. Because of the papillary reaction, prednisolone acetate, 1%, twice a day for 2 weeks was prescribed.
10. After 3 months, the symptoms had improved in the left eye, but conjunctival follicles were still present in the right inferior palpebral conjunctiva (Figure 1).
11. The patient subsequently underwent testing for chlamydia and gonorrhea, and the result was negative.
12. At the 1-year follow-up, the examination findings were unchanged.
13. During this follow-up, Lyme disease and Epstein-Barr virus serologic tests were performed in addition to repeated chlamydia testing.
14. The results were negative, except for a positive Epstein-Barr virus IgG.
15. Slitlamp photograph showing prominent large follicles (arrowhead) in the right inferior palpebral conjunctiva.

11. Surgical excision of the mediastinal mass was performed; its histopathologic features were consistent with a type AB thymoma, Masaoka-Koga stage 2A.A, Lacy, white erosive lesions on the tongue.

9. She demonstrated sluggish but reactive pupils and new-onset ophthalmoplegia.  
10. She was unable to move either eye in any direction, including with doll’s head maneuver.  
11. She was readmitted to the hospital and demonstrated diminished reflexes bilaterally and unsteady gait.  
12. Repeat magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated diffuse enhancement of the lower thoracic and cauda equina nerve roots and enhancement of the left oculomotor nerve (Figure).  
13. Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine (A) showing diffuse enhancement of the lower thoracic and equina nerve roots and of the brain (B) showing asymmetric enhancement of the left oculomotor nerve (arrowhead).

2. Her ophthalmic history was significant for mixed-mechanism glaucoma due to uveitis and chronic angle closure with prior implantation of bilateral superotemporal Baerveldt drainage implants.
3. Her intraocular pressure (IOP) was controlled with topical brinzolamide.
4. In addition, she had Fuchs corneal dystrophy.
5. A month earlier, she had undergone Baerveldt implant repositioning from the anterior chamber to the sulcus in the right eye in preparation for future Descemet stripping endothelial keratoplasty owing to severe corneal decompensation.
6. At that time, visual acuity was counting fingers at 1 ft OD.
7. She was discharged with therapy including topical steroids, antibiotics, and atropine sulfate.
8. On the first postoperative visit, IOP was 14 mm Hg OD by Goldmann applanation.
9. On postoperative day 11, IOP remained stable at 7 mm Hg OD by Goldmann applanation and topical atropine was discontinued.
10. At presentation 3 weeks postoperatively, IOP was 30 mm Hg OD by Goldmann applanation.
11. Her visual acuity worsened from counting fingers to hand motions.
12. Slitlamp examination of the right eye revealed a superotemporal Baerveldt drainage implant with fluid over the plate.
13. High-resolution ultrasonography was performed (Figure).High-resolution B-scan ultrasonographic image of the right eye.
14. White arrowheads indicate the anterior and posterior borders of the tube; magenta arrowhead, the lumen of the tube; AC, anterior chamber; and C, cornea.

Patient_Profile:
1. A 60-year-old man with advanced melanoma presented with headaches and increasing fatigue during treatment with ipilimumab.
2. Several months earlier, he presented to the emergency department with shortness of breath.
3. Imaging revealed pulmonary emboli and incidental groin lymphadenopathy.
4. Biopsy of a lymph node showed melanoma.
5. He then underwent inguinal lymph node dissection and was found to have 9 lymph nodes involved with melanoma (stage IIIC melanoma).He was then treated with ipilimumab (3 mg/kg), a monoclonal antibody to cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4), every 3 weeks, as part of an investigational adjuvant therapy clinical trial.
6. When presenting for his fourth and final dose of ipilimumab, he reported central headaches, severe fatigue, poor appetite, intermittent nausea, and a mild rash.
7. On examination, vital signs were within normal limits.
8. Physical examination had largely unremarkable results except for a slightly red, raised rash over his chest and proximal extremities.Laboratory testing showed the following: thyrotropin, 0.02 mIU/L (reference range, 0.3-5.0 mIU/L), and free thyroxine, less than 0.25 ng/dL (reference range, 0.5-1.2 ng/dL; to convert to picomoles per liter, multiply by 12.871).
9. Cosyntropin stimulation test showed a cortisol peak level of 0.9 µg/dL (reference range, >20 µg/dL; to convert to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 27.588).
10. He had low corticotropin (<5 pg/mL; reference range, 7-51 pg/mL; to convert to picomoles per liter, multiply by 0.22) and testosterone levels (<0.1 ng/mL; reference range, 2-11 ng/mL; to convert to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 0.0347).
11. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain is shown in the Figure.

1. A 31-year-old man presented with left cervical and left inguinal masses.
2. He reported intermittent itching and night sweats for 2 years.
3. He denied fever, weight loss, shortness of breath, rashes, diarrhea, and neurological symptoms.
4. On a preemployment evaluation, the patient was told he had a high white blood cell count 2 years ago.
5. On examination, there was left cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy and no other organomegaly.
6. Complete blood cell count and peripheral blood smear showed marked leukocytosis, with a white blood cell count of 22 340/μL, an absolute neutrophil count of 5360/μL, and 55% eosinophils with an absolute eosinophil count of 12 290/μL (to convert all to cells ×109/L, multiply by 0.001).
7. Vitamin B12 was markedly elevated at more than 4000 pg/mL (to convert to pmol/L, multiply by 0.7378).
8. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 5 mm/h.
9. Lactate dehydrogenase was 180 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase was 81 U/L (to convert both to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167).
10. Evaluations for HIV and hepatitis B and C were all negative.
11. Serum creatinine was 0.76 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4); alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase were 11 U/L and 9.9 U/L, respectively (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167); and total bilirubin was 0.35 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 17.104).
12. Bone marrow biopsy showed hypercellular marrow (cellularity of 100%), myeloid hyperplasia, increased eosinophils with some dysplasia, and a blast count of 2%.
13. Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan showed a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm and a left inguinal lymph node of 3.1 × 2.3 cm with an standardized uptake value max of 5.7 (Figure, A).
14. Left inguinal lymph node biopsy showed partial involvement by atypical cells with high proliferation index (Ki-67 >95%) that were positive for CD3, CD4, CD8, BCL2, and TDT, suggestive of T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia (Figure, B).A, Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic (PET/CT) scan of the head and neck at presentation showing a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm (arrowhead).
15. B, Lymph node biopsy immunohistochemical stain with terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase.
16. The inset shows interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization for FIP1L1::PDGFRA rearrangement (positive).
17. C, PET/CT 12 weeks after treatment initiation.Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions

1. A woman in her mid-20s presented with subacute bilateral vision loss that was worse in the left eye.  
2. Her medical history was remarkable for type 1 diabetes diagnosed at 16 years of age and proliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes that had been treated with panretinal photocoagulation 7 years earlier.  
3. She had undergone pars plana vitrectomy with endolaser to treat a tractional retinal detachment in her right eye 2 years before this presentation.  
4. She also had a history of hypertension and chronic kidney disease, and she was 15 weeks into pregnancy.  
5. Visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/100 OS.  
6. Intraocular pressure was normal bilaterally, and no relative afferent pupillary defect was detected.  
7. Findings of an anterior segment examination were normal.  
8. The patient was in no apparent distress and denied any headache, chest pain, or focal weakness.  
9. Ophthalmoscopic examination (Figure) revealed mild optic nerve head edema that was greater in the left eye than the right eye with associated nerve fiber layer hemorrhage in the left eye.  
10. Nerve fiber layer infarctions, dot and blot hemorrhages, and lesions caused by panretinal photocoagulation also were seen bilaterally.  
11. Optical coherence tomography showed macular edema that involved the center of the macula in both eyes (Figure, inset).  
12. Fundus photographs obtained at presentation that show bilateral peripapillary hemorrhages and mild optic nerve head edema.  
13. Insets show the corresponding optical coherence tomographic image.

2. She had neither fever nor skin redness but was experiencing fatigue.

8. She denied any trauma to the breast.

14. 1. A previously healthy 23-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of worsening pain, dynamic color changes, and ulcerations involving the fingertips of both hands.  
2. On review of systems, she reported hair loss, dryness of the eyes and mouth, and mild esophageal dysphagia.  
3. She reported no oral ulcers, pleuritic chest pain, shortness of breath, hemoptysis, decreased urine output, hematuria, joint pain, fevers, or weight change.  
4. On examination, she was afebrile.  
5. Heart rate was 60/min; blood pressure, 100/70 mm Hg; respiratory rate, 18/min; and Spo2, 100%.  
6. Her hands and fingers were mildly edematous, and the fingertips variably showed purple discoloration, distal pitting scars, and ischemic ulcers (Figure, panel A).  
7. There was periungual erythema with dilated nailfold capillaries but no splinter hemorrhages.  
8. She had no evidence of sclerodactyly or proximal skin thickening, with hands and face showing fine wrinkles and normal-appearing skin folds.  
9. Results of initial laboratory studies were notable for white blood cell count 3270/μL; hemoglobin level, 14.5 g/dL; platelet count, 143 ×103/μL; creatinine level, 1.0 mg/dL (88.4 μmol/L); and C-reactive protein level, 0.1 mg/dL.  
10. Computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the bilateral upper extremities showed normal vasculature.  
11. Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) were positive at 1:640 or greater by indirect immunofluorescence in a composite nuclear and nucleolar fine speckled staining pattern (Figure, B).  
12. Subserologic testing showed high positive anti-Ro52 (176; <20), anti-Ro60 (563; <20), and anti–Scl-70 antibodies (786; <20).

4. The chest radiographic findings and blood work results were unremarkable.
5. The lack of response to oral prednisone therapy led to suspicion of a possible malignant neoplasm, and the patient was referred for our opinion.
6. The patient’s medical history was notable for chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL) with transformation to large B-cell lymphoma that was treated with rituximab, adriamycin, vincristine sulfate, and prednisone chemotherapy 4 years earlier.
7. Two years before referral, bladder cancer was diagnosed and was treated surgically and with multiple rounds of intravesical BCG immunotherapy.

12. Bullae on patient’s right toes, anterior foot, and ankle (right).

Patient_Profile:
1. A well-appearing 14-month-old girl was referred for the evaluation of recurrent left subconjunctival hemorrhage with increasing frequency since 7 months of age.
2. Multiple prior office visits with referring ophthalmologists during which eyes were dilated showed normal results.
3. Clinical examination revealed 180° of left interior subconjunctival hemorrhage with overlying conjunctival elevation and mild fullness of the left lower eyelid (Figure 1A).
4. Fixation was central, steady, and maintained bilaterally, with full ocular motility and absence of appreciable proptosis.
5. Penlight anterior segment examination demonstrated normally formed anterior segment structures without inflammation or hyphema in either eye, although the left eye exhibited a small intraocular lightly pigmented lesion at the 5-o'clock limbus.
6. Examination under anesthesia (EUA) was deemed appropriate and further demonstrated normal intraocular pressures bilaterally.
7. Handheld slitlamp examination localized the left eye 2-mm limbal lesion on the posterior corneal surface.
8. The surrounding corneal and iris structures were normal appearing without evidence of vascularization.
9. Ultrasound biomicroscopy was used to further evaluate both the intraocular lesion and better characterize the left lower eyelid fullness.
10. This demonstrated no iris, angle, or ciliary body involvement by the intraocular lesion.
11. A 10-MHz contact B-scan examination showed a large inferior orbital lesion measuring more than 17 mm in the anterior-to-posterior dimension (Figure 1B).
12. Doppler ultrasonography did not demonstrate significant flow to suggest a vascular cause.
13. Clinical photograph of a subconjunctival hemorrhage of the left eye (A) and B-scan image of an orbital mass (B).

4. Twelve years prior, he underwent uncomplicated Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) surgery.
5. Review of systems was notable for fatigue and negative for fever, night sweats, weight loss, dyspnea, or abnormal bleeding.

12. Peripheral blood smear showed occasional pseudo Pelger-Huet cells and rare teardrop cells.
13. 14. Cytogenetic studies from the bone marrow did not reveal any abnormalities.
15. Histopathologic examination of bone marrow aspirate from patient (A, Wright-Giemsa, original magnification ×1000; B, Prussian blue iron, original magnification ×1000).

14. The skin lesions were dome-shaped papules, round, pinkish-white in color, surrounded by an erythematous area.  
15. Full blood cell count and tests for HIV, AIDS, and syphilis were ordered.  
16. Conjunctival swabs and eyelid vesicle fluid were taken for polymerase chain reaction testing.

1. A 53-year-old man received a diagnosis of stage IV melanoma with metastatic disease to the spine and brain 3 months before presentation.
2. Four weeks following receipt of immunotherapy with ipilimumab and nivolumab, he developed acute abdominal pain in the setting of a rapidly rising lactic acid dehydrogenase levels, prompting hospital admission.
3. Imaging results showed mild disease progression (new ascites and periportal metabolic lymph node).
4. Splenic infarct and portal/splenic vein thrombi were identified as etiologies of his acute pain and were presumed to be secondary to hypercoagulable state of malignancy.
5. Over the next 3 days, he had rising serum creatinine (sCr) levels (baseline, approximately 1 mg/dL [to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4]).
6. The initial workup included ultrasonography and urinalysis.
7. Ultrasonography results showed abnormal intraparenchymal flow to both kidneys without evidence of kidney artery stenosis.
8. Urine studies were consistent with prerenal etiology, while the presence of casts suggested acute tubular necrosis.
9. Nephrotoxic medications (omeprazole/pantoprazole) were discontinued.
10. The top differential diagnoses at this juncture included contrast-induced nephropathy or immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)–induced acute interstitial nephritis, and empirical high dose steroids were prescribed.
11. Despite observation and steroid treatment, his sCr levels continued to increase over the next 5 days, peaking at 5.8 mg/dL, and the patient progressed into anuric kidney failure, requiring hemodialysis.
12. This prompted a kidney biopsy for definitive diagnosis (Figure).
13. One week later, he received encorafenib, a BRAF inhibitor.
14. Two weeks later, the patient’s kidney function began to improve, and hemodialysis was discontinued.
15. He continued to show gradual improvement, with a return to near baseline kidney function (sCr level, 1.3 mg/dL) approximately 6 weeks after treatment initiation.
16. Histopathology (original magnification x40) of kidney capillaries with hematoxylin and eosin stain showing atypical cells (arrowheads) (A), tubules with hematoxylin and eosin stain (B), and capillaries with melanin-A (C).

1. A man in his 80s presented with 3 months of painless progressive vision loss, followed by gait changes, memory loss, and 10-lb unintentional weight loss.

6. Extraocular movements were full with gaze-evoked nystagmus.
7. Horizontal vestibulo-ocular reflex, assessed by head impulse testing, was normal.
8. Slitlamp and dilated fundus examination revealed pseudophakia and mild epiretinal membrane in the right eye and mild nuclear sclerosis in the left eye.
9. Goldmann perimetry (V4e stimulus) of left (A) and right (B) eyes shows right homonymous hemianopia, left inferotemporal visual field loss, and right nasal paracentral visual field loss.
10. Neurologic examination showed full motor strength, decreased vibration sense and proprioception in the feet, positive Romberg sign, and inability to tandem walk.
11. Mini-Mental State Examination score was 6 of 30.
12. Magnetic resonance imaging brain and orbits with and without contrast and magnetic resonance angiography head and neck were unremarkable.
13. An electroencephalogram showed no localizing signs.
14. Syphilis screen was negative.
15. Serum thiamine, vitamin B12, and thyrotropin levels were normal.
16. Cerebrospinal fluid composition, infectious studies, cytology, flow cytometry, and paraneoplastic panel showed only mildly elevated protein.

8. On examination, he had right-sided ptosis and severe right facial weakness in a lower motor neuron pattern with temporal wasting.
9. The right pupil was fixed and dilated.
10. There was no afferent pupillary defect.
11. The left pupil was appropriately sized and reactive.
12. His right-sided vision was impaired (20/250) with blurriness.
13. Vertical and horizontal binocular diplopia was present.
14. Right extraocular movements were significantly limited in all directions and painful, and right-sided facial sensation was diminished to pinprick in all cranial nerve (CN) V distributions.
15. His speech was slightly slurred.
16. Left-sided extraocular movements were intact.
17. His left facial sensation was intact to pinprick, and his strength was without deficit.
18. There were no other neurological abnormalities.
19. Initial magnetic resonance images (MRIs) were unremarkable.
20. A biopsy of CN VII was nondiagnostic.
21. Hemoglobin A1c was 6.8%.
22. Tests for infection and autoimmune disease had negative results.
23. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies showed mildly elevated protein values.
24. Figure 1 shows the MRI at presentation.

1. A 50-year-old woman presented to the emergency department for 3 months of right orbital pain.
2. Her medical history was noncontributory.
3. Examination revealed a right afferent pupillary defect, visual acuity of hand motion OD and 20/30 OS, full extraocular movements, and bilateral retinal dot blot hemorrhages.
4. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed enhancement along the right intracanalicular optic nerve and adjacent sinuses (Figure).
5. Glycosylated hemoglobin level was elevated at 10.3% (to convert to proportion of total hemoglobin, multiply by 0.01).

7. A, Contrast enhancement centered on the right intracanalicular optic nerve (blue arrowhead), involving right orbital apex and posterior ethmoidal sinus (white arrowhead).

9. Specimen cultures grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA).
10. The patient was diagnosed as having type 2 diabetes and MSSA sino-orbital infection.
11. She was discharged 10 days later with intravenous (IV) antibacterials, sitagliptin, insulin, and oral opiates.The patient returned to the emergency department 2 weeks later with recurrent orbital pain.
12. Although examination was stable, MRI showed increased apical enhancement.
13. The diagnosis was revised to nonspecific orbital inflammation and the neurology department initiated a 3-day course of IV methylprednisolone.
14. Pain rapidly resolved, repeated MRI showed reduced enhancement, and she was discharged with a prednisone taper.Ten days later, the patient returned once again to the emergency department with pain.
15. Although imaging was stable, examination revealed visual acuity of no light perception OD and new-onset right-sided third, fourth, and sixth cranial neuropathies.

1. A woman in her 50s presented with an edematous, massively enlarged right auricle.

10. 3. He reported having normal bowel movements and passing flatus without difficulty.
4. On examination, he was afebrile and not tachycardic.
5. He had a well-healed abdominal midline wound.
6. His abdomen was soft, not distended, and mildly tender diffusely, worse in the epigastrium, without rebound, guarding, or any palpable masses.
7. His bloodwork revealed an elevated lipase level of 2842 U/L (to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167) without leukocytosis or any electrolyte abnormalities.

9. Given a history of pancreaticoduodenectomy, the patient underwent computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with oral and intravenous contrast for further evaluation (Figure).
10. A, Axial cross-section of patient's computed tomographic scan of his abdomen and pelvis after a Whipple procedure.
11. The stomach is distended with oral contrast and an air fluid level.
12. A tubular solid structure can be seen within the body of the stomach.
13. B, Coronal view demonstrating the tubular solid mass within the distended stomach.

2. Her symptoms began 6 hours before presentation after she had been napping face-down on her desk for 30 minutes.
3. Her medical history included aortic repair and cervical spine abnormalities.
4. Her ocular history was pertinent for high myopia and contact lens wear, a posteriorly dislocated crystalline lens suspended in the vitreous cavity in her right eye, and a superotemporally subluxated crystalline lens in her left eye.
5. Her lenses had been observed for years without intervention.
6. The patient’s family history was unknown because she was adopted.
7. Her medications included oral aspirin and irbesartan.
8. Visual acuity was counting fingers OD (without correction) and 20/30 OS (with correction).
9. The right pupil was corectopic and fixed at 5 mm while the left pupil was round and reactive; no afferent pupillary defect was seen.
10. Extraocular motility was normal.
11. Intraocular pressures (IOPs) were 43 mm Hg OD and 14 mm Hg OS.
12. Examination of the right eye revealed conjunctival injection, corneal stromal edema with Descemet folds and lenticulocorneal touch, a shallowed anterior chamber, and a lens protruding through the pupil with the superior edge in the anterior chamber (Figure 1A).
13. The posterior view was limited to red reflex.
14. The left eye was unremarkable except for a superotemporally subluxated lens (Figure 1B).
15. Slitlamp photography.
16. A, Right eye demonstrates dislocation of the superior crystalline lens into the anterior chamber.
17. B, Left eye shows superotemporal subluxation of the crystalline lens.
18. The remaining zonules are visualized inferior to the lens as wispy white strands.
19. Instill atropine and IOP-lowering drops and place the patient in a supine position

Patient_Profile:
1. A woman in her 30s was referred for evaluation of corneal opacities.
2. Her medical history was notable for keratoconjunctivitis sicca, Hashimoto thyroiditis, and anti–interferon-γ autoantibody syndrome treated with 6 monthly rituximab infusions (375 mg/m2 with 100 mg of methylprednisolone acetate).
3. Infusions were given weekly for the first 3 weeks and then every 6 to 8 months based on a CD20 count.
4. She had previously been diagnosed with disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection requiring 2 years of treatment with rifabutin, 300 mg/d; ethambutol hydrochloride, 1000 mg/d; and clarithromycin in a divided dose, 500 mg twice a day.
5. This treatment concluded 2½ years before presentation.
6. In addition, she had a long-standing history of arthralgias with intermittent arthritis treated with hydroxychloroquine, 300 mg/d, that was discontinued 2 years before presentation.
7. On examination, she had no visual concerns.
8. Her visual acuity was 20/20 OU.
9. Conjunctivas were normal, lenses were clear, and anterior chambers were deep and quiet.
10. The results from the slitlamp examination showed numerous bilateral, peripheral light brown corneal opacities.
11. The opacities were located in the far posterior corneae and were present circumferentially (Figure, A).
12. There was no associated keratitis or corneal neovascularization.
13. Anterior segment optical coherence tomographic findings showed focal areas of hyperreflectivity anterior to the Descemet membrane.
14. Confocal microscopy revealed variably shaped, hyperreflective clusters of opacities just anterior to the endothelium (Figure, B).
15. Imaging of the right eye of a patient with rifabutin-related posterior corneal deposits.
16. A, Slitlamp photograph with arrowhead highlighting one of numerous bilateral peripheral, small corneal light brown opacities.
17. B, Confocal microscopic image captured at a slightly oblique angle illustrates normal endothelial cells (yellow arrowhead).
18. Just anterior to the endothelium, the drug deposit appears as variably shaped, hyperreflective clusters of opacities (white arrowhead).

Patient_Profile:
1. A 41-year-old woman with a history of ocular hypertension (and using brimonidine tartrate and timolol maleate) was referred by her ophthalmologist for a second opinion regarding yellowish subfoveal precipitates in her left eye.
2. Three months earlier, she had undergone pneumatic retinopexy for macula-on retinal detachment (RD) with a superotemporal tear, followed by vitrectomy with gas injection for macula-on inferonasal detachment 1 month later.
3. She had persistent postoperative subretinal fluid inferonasally, and she was concerned about a central scotoma.
4. An examination within 2 months of the vitrectomy revealed yellowish subfoveal precipitates.
5. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/200 OS.
6. Extraocular motility was full, but she displayed left exotropia.
7. Confrontational visual fields were full for the right eye but showed a decreased field inferiorly for the left eye.
8. Intraocular pressures as determined using Tonopen tonometry were 13 mm Hg OD and 12 mm Hg OS.
9. A slitlamp examination revealed trace nuclear sclerosis and pigmented cells in the anterior vitreous of the left eye.
10. An ophthalmoscopic examination indicated laser and cryotherapy scars 360° around a horseshoe tear superotemporally in the left eye, whereas the right eye appeared normal.
11. In addition, pre-equatorial subretinal fluid in the left eye between the 6-o’clock and 8:30 position was associated with 2 tiny holes at the 7:30 position and with a small area of fibrotic tissue contraction consistent with early proliferative vitreoretinopathy.
12. The macula had yellow-white, flat, vitelliform-like lesions with a surrounding high watermark (Figure).
13. No cyst, exudate, or hemorrhage was detected in the macula.

1. A 45-year-old woman presented to the emergency department on the morning after Thanksgiving with sudden, severe, constant epigastric pain that migrated to the right upper quadrant as well as subjective fever and emesis since the previous evening.
2. She reported a failure to pass stool or flatus since the onset of symptoms.
3. She denied hematochezia, melena, or hematemesis.
4. Her medical history was significant for heavy smoking, reflux, and surgical procedures including a right inguinal hernia repair, total abdominal hysterectomy, and bilateral salpingo-oopherectomy, all more than 5 years prior.
5. On examination, she had a distended and tympanic abdomen with tenderness, guarding, and rebound in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant.
6. Vital signs and standard laboratory test results were unremarkable.
7. An upright abdominal plain radiograph showed a distended, thickened stomach and multiple dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels.
8. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated a focal area of mixed fat density involving the distal small bowel concerning for a lead point with adjacent mesenteric fat stranding (Figure 1).
9. The scan also revealed multiple bilateral lung nodules.
10. Computed tomography of abdomen.
11. A, Coronal view demonstrating obstructing intraluminal lesion (arrowhead).
12. B, Transverse view demonstrating obstructing intraluminal lesion (arrowhead).
13. The patient was subsequently taken to the operating room for exploratory laparotomy and found to have an obstruction in the distal ileum.

Patient_Profile:
1. A 24-year-old South Asian man presented with acute-onset pain and decreased vision in his left eye.  
2. His ocular history was significant for high myopia, a long-standing traumatic retinal detachment in his right eye, and laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) surgery of the left eye 8 months earlier.  
3. Three months earlier, the patient experienced an episode of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) of the left eye, which was treated with travoprost ophthalmic solution, 0.004%, and oral acetazolamide and resolved.  
4. The patient’s presenting visual acuity was counting fingers OD (baseline) and 20/200 OS.  
5. His initial IOPs were right eye 16 mm Hg and left eye 46 mm Hg by TonoPen.  
6. Examination of the left eye indicated normal gonioscopy results and unremarkable anterior and posterior segment examination findings except for the presence of corneal edema without keratic precipitates.  
7. The patient started treatment with dorzolamide hydrochloride, timolol maleate, brimonidine tartrate, latanoprost, and oral acetazolamide.  
8. The next day, the left eye IOP improved to 28 mm Hg as measured by Goldmann applanation tonometry (GAT), with a clear cornea and return of visual acuity to 20/20.  
9. Despite continuing maximum medical therapy for 1 week, the patient’s examination findings remained unchanged.  
10. Because of a concern for possible trabeculitis, he also started treatment with topical prednisolone acetate 4 times daily and oral valacyclovir hydrochloride.  
11. Two days later, the patient returned to the clinic with decreased vision in his left eye, which showed an IOP measured by GAT of 6 mm Hg, visual acuity of 20/400, and a cornea that was edematous (Figure 1).  
12. A, Slitlamp photograph showing a prominent laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) flap in the patient’s left eye.  
13. B, A slit beam focused on the cornea reveals a shallow fluid interface between the stromal bed and the LASIK flap (arrowheads).

1. A 63-year-old white man with a history of cigarette use (≥80 pack-years) and alcohol dependence presented to the ophthalmology clinic with several weeks of left eye pain and redness.
2. A review of systems was remarkable for unintentional weight loss, night sweats, and cough with scant sputum.
3. On presentation, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OU.
4. Intraocular pressure, pupillary reaction, and ocular motility were normal.
5. The right eye had normal anterior and posterior segment examination findings.
6. The left eye was notable for mostly superior conjunctival and scleral hyperemia with dilated scleral vessels and associated scleral thinning with a conjunctival epithelial defect (Figure 1).
7. The results of posterior examination of the left eye were normal.
8. Results of serologic tests, including Treponema pallidum particle agglutination assay, HIV, hepatitis B and C, Lyme antibody, rheumatoid factor, and anticyclic citrullinated peptide, were negative.
9. Angiotensin-converting enzyme level, uric acid level, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, complete blood cell count, and basic metabolic panel results were within normal limits.
10. The results of proteinase 3–antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) testing and interferon γ release assay using QuantiFERON-TB gold (QFT) (Qiagen) were positive.
11. Chest computed tomography revealed tiny, scattered solid pulmonary nodules that were too small to characterize according to the radiology department.
12. The patient was referred to the infectious diseases clinic, where the results of sputum culture and polymerase chain reaction for Mycobacteria tuberculosis were negative.
13. Pulmonology evaluation determined that the pulmonary nodules were too small for biopsy via bronchoscopy.Slitlamp photograph of the left eye shows diffuse hyperemia with dilated vessels and scleral thinning.
14. Initiate rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (RIPE) therapy

8. His visual acuity could not be determined.

10. The eyelids were mildly erythematous with bilateral eyelash hypertrichosis.  
11. The conjunctiva and cornea appeared dry and leathery bilaterally.  
12. The right cornea was diffusely hazy with a 3-mm paracentral epithelial defect with 60% stromal thinning and a 1-mm infiltrate.  
13. There was a small crescentic fibrin deposit nasally in the right anterior chamber.  
14. The left cornea was diffusely hazy with a 1-mm epithelial defect without stromal thinning (Figure).  
15. Dilated examination showed bilateral grade 3 optic nerve head edema and otherwise normal retinal findings.  
16. Fortified vancomycin eye drops, 25 mg/mL, and tobramycin eye drops, 15 mg/mL, were initiated.  
17. Results of magnetic resonance imaging of the brain were normal.  
18. Photographs of the right (A) and left (B) eyes reveal a dry and lusterless appearance of the conjunctivae and corneas of both eyes.  
19. There were bilateral corneal epithelial defects with 60% stromal thinning in the right eye (arrowhead).

11. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody testing revealed elevated proteinase 3 antibody level.
12. In the setting of anemia, infectious-disease consultants raised concern for babesiosis.
13. Peripheral blood smear and polymerase chain reaction were performed; empirical therapy of azithromycin, 500 mg daily, plus atovaquone, 750 mg twice daily, was initiated.

2. His medical history included squamous cell carcinoma of the lung diagnosed 1 year prior, which was resected.  
3. On examination, his visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/25 OS and he had mutton fat keratic precipitates and 1+ cells in both eyes.  
4. The vitreous and retina revealed no signs of inflammation.  
5. The day before, he had undergone a positron emission tomography scan to look for evidence of metastatic lung cancer.  
6. The result revealed mild to moderate diffuse lymphadenopathy in the neck, axillae, mediastinal, and inguinal regions.  
7. The symmetric pattern favored a diagnosis of sarcoidosis; metastatic disease was less likely.  
8. Because the scan was consistent with a diagnosis of sarcoidosis in this patient with granulomatous anterior iritis, no further laboratory testing was pursued.  
9. The patient started treatment with prednisolone acetate, 1%, 4 times daily in both eyes.  
10. A lymph-node biopsy showed lymphoid follicular hyperplasia and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation, consistent with sarcoidosis.  
11. There was no evidence of lymphoma.  
12. The results of special stains were negative for bartonella, fungal organisms, and mycobacterial infection (Figure 1A).

14. B, Fundus photograph of the right eye with 3+ vitreous haze and retinitis.  
15. C, Fundus photograph of the left eye with retinitis, serous retinal detachment, and disc hyperemia.  
16. The patient returned with loss of vision in his right eye.  
17. On examination, his visual acuity was counting fingers OD and 20/30 OS.  
18. He had 2+ cells in the anterior chamber and 3+ vitreous haze (Figure 1B).  
19. He was treated with prednisone, 60 mg daily, for sarcoid panuveitis.  
20. One week later, he had vision loss in both eyes.  
21. His visual acuity was hand motions OD and counting fingers OS.

6. 10. After returning to the United States, he developed dyspnea with exertion.
11. He was found to have an ejection fraction (EF) of 20% to 25% with 4-chamber dilation and was diagnosed with cardiomyopathy.
12. Results of limited infectious workup, including blood and stool cultures and tests for leptospirosis and dengue fever, were negative.

Patient_Profile:
1. A woman in her 80s with a history of nonischemic cardiomyopathy and chronic kidney disease presented with purpuric lesions on her face, elbows, knees, and feet.
2. She was initially admitted for altered mental status in the setting of an unwitnessed fall and was noted to have “bruises” on her lower extremities.
3. Dermatology was consulted after the development of new lesions on her nose, ear, and the extensor surfaces of her arms bilaterally.
4. Admission laboratory test results showed hypercalcemia (calcium level, 11.5 mg/dL) and acute kidney injury (creatinine level, 5.6 mg/dL).
5. On physical examination, the patient’s nose, bilateral cheeks, forehead, and left ear (helical rim and antihelix [Figure, A]) were found to have dusky purpuric macules and patches.
6. Her knees, feet, and the extensor surfaces of her arms had reticulated purpuric macules and patches.
7. There was skin sloughing off the lesions on her elbows (Figure, B) and knees.
8. Four-millimeter punch biopsy specimens were taken from the left ear, right arm, and forehead (Figure, C and D).
9. Clinical and histopathologic images from a case of acral retiform purpura.
10. A, Dusky purpuric macules on the helical rim and antihelix of the ear.
11. B, Reticulated purpuric patches with focal areas of necrosis on the extensor surfaces of the arms.
12. C and D, In specimens from the forehead, multifocal intravascular fibrinoid material consisting of a mix of cryoglobulins and fibrin thrombi with relatively little vessel wall inflammation was seen (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×4 [C] and ×10 [D]).

2. The infant was born to a 31-year-old mother by normal vaginal delivery.  
3. The mother had a benign prenatal course during pregnancy.  
4. Since the rash developed, the infant had been fussy with increasing restlessness at night.  
5. The parents denied any personal or family history of rash.  
6. On further questioning, the parents reported that the infant had had contact with a babysitter who reported pruritus, especially at night.  
7. The sitter had provided domestic care for the infant since birth until leaving that position 3 weeks earlier.  
8. On examination, the infant was afebrile with normal vital signs.  
9. Multiple disseminated, edematous, pin-sized, papulopustulovesicles and 5- to 10-mm coalescing, crusted nodules were found all over the body; some with oval to elongated, serpiginous or J-shaped burrows (Figure 1).  
10. No excoriations were visible.  
11. A Tzanck smear showed no multinucleated giant cells in the pustular contents.  
12. A Gram stain and potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of the pustular contents showed no bacterial or fungal elements.  
13. Cultures of the pustular contents yielded no bacterial or fungal growth.  
14. The differential of a complete blood cell count showed 12% eosinophils.  
15. Results of other routine laboratory investigations were unremarkable.

1. A man in his 40s was referred for a 1-year history of decreased vision and the sensation of tunnel vision, which accompanied cognitive decline for the past 2 years.
2. He had a history of renal cell carcinoma and had undergone left nephrectomy 1 year prior with no recurrence.
3. Prior to presentation, his evaluation included brain magnetic resonance imaging and neurologic evaluation with unremarkable results, and he was scheduled to undergo neuropsychological testing.
4. Visual acuity was counting fingers OD, and 20/100 OS.
5. Motility and intraocular pressures were normal.
6. There was a right afferent pupillary defect.
7. Examination of the right eye revealed rubeosis iridis, a clear lens, neovascularization of the optic disc, retinal vasculitis, venous sheathing, and a dusky-appearing peripheral retina.
8. The left eye had a clear lens and a normal fundus on clinical examination.
